standard.title: Continuing Struggles for Rights
standard.description: the continuing efforts to create change in the civil rights and freedoms in Australia, for First Nations Australians, migrants and women
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have examined First Nations rights campaigns and civil rights events (K09–K11), the women's movement (K12), and changing attitudes to migration (K08). They have evaluated the extent of change in each domain and identified limits. They have not yet examined the three domains together as a connected pattern of ongoing struggle, or examined the international frameworks that support continuing rights claims.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain continuing efforts to create change in civil rights and freedoms for First Nations Australians, migrants, and women, and examine Australia's responsibilities under international human rights frameworks.

nodes.label: The gap between formal rights and lived reality
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the concept of the gap between formal legal rights and lived experience, and apply it to all three groups as a unifying analytical framework.
nodes.minimum_width: Students explain the formal-rights–lived-reality gap and apply it to at least two of the three groups with a specific example from each.
nodes.typical_width: Students establish the analytical framework — formal legal equality does not automatically produce social equality; structural conditions, cultural attitudes, and institutional practices can maintain inequality even after legal barriers are removed; apply this to First Nations Australians (1967 Referendum → Closing the Gap data), to women (Sex Discrimination Act → gender pay gap, domestic violence rates), and to migrants (Racial Discrimination Act → lived experiences of racism and discrimination); explain why the gap persists in each case.
wider: Examine why the gap between formal rights and lived reality persists — analysing competing explanations (structural racism, cultural attitudes, economic inequality, institutional inertia) and what each implies for what further change is needed
Investigate how international human rights frameworks define this gap — examining the difference between de jure rights (formally recognised) and de facto rights (actually experienced)
nodes.hinge_reason: The formal-rights–lived-reality gap is the conceptual framework that explains why continuing struggle is necessary despite legislative gains. Students who lack this framework cannot explain why campaigns continue after formal legal changes have been achieved — they treat the ongoing struggle as irrational or as evidence that change has not occurred.

response_modes.reason: Students commonly assume that legal change ends discrimination. The scaffold is: what did the legal change achieve formally? what did it not change in practice? what structural or cultural conditions maintain the gap? This reframes continuing struggle as rational and necessary rather than as evidence of insufficient progress.

success_criteria: Explains the formal-rights–lived-reality gap as an analytical concept
Applies it to at least two of the three groups with a specific example from each
Explains at least one structural or cultural condition that maintains the gap

nodes.label: Continuing struggles — First Nations Australians
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify the focus areas of continuing civil rights action for First Nations Australians and explain why ongoing action remains necessary.
nodes.minimum_width: Students identify at least three focus areas for continuing First Nations rights action and explain why each remains a site of struggle.
nodes.typical_width: Students examine the focus areas — education, health care, housing, employment, incarceration rates, child removal (under child protection legislation), land rights implementation; connect each to the formal-rights gap from N1; explain why the gap persists in each domain despite the legal changes achieved since 1967; examine the Uluru Statement from the Heart's three demands (Voice, Treaty, Truth) as the current framework for continuing action; explain UNDRIP (2007) and Australia's responsibilities as a signatory.
wider: Examine the Northern Territory Intervention (2007) — analysing how it was justified, how it affected First Nations communities, and whether it represented an advance or a regression in rights

Investigate the over-representation of First Nations Australians in the criminal justice system as a case study in structural inequality — using the Royal Commission into Deaths in Custody (1991) findings to examine whether recommendations have been implemented
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The NT Intervention and the Deaths in Custody data are analytically rich — they connect historical patterns to present-day outcomes and require students to evaluate whether government action has advanced or undermined rights, which is a genuine analytical question with contested answers.

response_modes.reason: Examining multiple focus areas prevents the reduction of continuing First Nations rights action to a single issue and builds the evidential base for arguing why ongoing action is necessary.

success_criteria: Identifies at least three focus areas for continuing First Nations rights action with specific evidence for each
Explains why each area remains a site of struggle — connecting to the formal-rights gap

nodes.label: Continuing struggles — women and migrants
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the continuing efforts to advance women's rights and migrants' rights, connecting each to the formal-rights gap and to relevant legislative frameworks.
nodes.minimum_width: Students explain at least two areas of continuing struggle for women and at least one for migrants, connecting each to the formal-rights gap.
nodes.typical_width: Students examine continuing women's rights issues — reproductive rights, domestic and family violence (rates, legislative responses, adequacy), political representation (proportion of women in parliament over time), gender pay gap persistence; examine the Racial Discrimination Act 1975 as the legal framework for migrant rights and its limits in practice; examine continuing debates over asylum seeker rights, temporary protection visas, and the treatment of refugees; connect each to the N1 framework.
wider: Examine Australia's gender pay gap using current ABS data — evaluating whether the legislative framework established in the 1970s–80s has been adequate and what structural reforms are proposed

Investigate the legal status of asylum seekers under Australian law and international law — analysing the tension between Australia's Refugee Convention obligations and its domestic border protection policies

response_modes.reason: Covering both women's and migrants' continuing struggles in the same node shows students that the pattern of formal-rights–lived-reality gaps applies across groups — this is the generalisation that gives N1's framework its analytical power.

success_criteria: Explains at least two areas of continuing struggle for women with evidence
Explains at least one area of continuing struggle for migrants, connecting to relevant legislation
Connects each area to the formal-rights–lived-reality gap from N1

nodes.label: International frameworks and Australia's obligations
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the role of international human rights frameworks in supporting continuing rights claims, including UNDRIP, the Racial Discrimination Act, and Australia's responsibilities as a signatory to international conventions.
nodes.minimum_width: Students explain how at least one international framework supports continuing rights claims in Australia; explain what obligations Australia has as a signatory.
nodes.typical_width: Students examine UNDRIP (2007) — its content, Australia's initial refusal to sign and later endorsement, what it requires of Australia regarding First Nations rights; examine the Racial Discrimination Act 1975 as the domestic expression of international anti-discrimination norms; explain how international frameworks set a floor for rights claims that domestic law must meet or exceed; evaluate the gap between Australia's international commitments and its domestic practice; examine how advocacy groups use international frameworks to hold governments accountable.
wider: Examine how Australian First Nations groups have used international forums — including the UN Human Rights Committee and the Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination — to draw attention to failures in domestic rights protection
Evaluate whether international human rights frameworks have been effective in advancing rights for the three groups studied — assessing the mechanisms of enforcement and their limits
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The use of international forums by domestic rights groups is a sophisticated analytical topic that connects K13 to broader questions about international law, sovereignty, and accountability — and provides a clear example of how historical knowledge of rights movements connects to contemporary practice.

response_modes.reason: This node integrates the three-group continuing struggles (N2–N3) and the formal-rights framework (N1) into an account of how international obligations shape the ongoing rights landscape. Tasks requiring students to connect domestic struggles to international frameworks work well here.

success_criteria: Explains how at least one international framework supports continuing rights claims in Australia
Explains what obligations Australia has as a signatory to that framework
Evaluates the gap between Australia's international commitments and domestic practice in at least one area
